concepts.title: Robustness vs. accuracy tradeoff
concepts.one_liner: Hand-crafted models offer high accuracy within specific assumptions, while learning-based models provide greater robustness and generalization across diverse conditions.
concepts.content:
While hand-crafted algorithms can produce highly accurate 3D reconstructions when images fit specific world assumptions, they are often fragile. For instance, poor illumination can break edge detectors, resulting in a cascade of errors. A hand-crafted approach may completely fail if a small change occurs, such as changing the ground plane color. 

(see figure: 3D reconstruction using the simple visual system from @sec-simplesystem)

In contrast, learning-based models like MiDaS may lose some precision—cubes' edges might not be perfectly straight or surfaces perfectly flat—but they gain significantly in robustness and generalization. These models produce results of consistent quality regardless of conditions, even when applied to simple worlds dissimilar to their natural-image training data.

(see figure: Out of domain generalization. For the pretrained model, these images might still be within the domain of the training, as it contained a very diverse set of natural images. The simple system model...)
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains the fundamental tension between specialized precision and general-purpose reliability. It helps engineers decide whether to use rigid, rule-based systems or flexible, data-driven models based on the variability of the environment.

  "- Learning-based models generalize better to new domains and offer higher robustness at the cost of some geometric accuracy."

concepts.title: LLM-based scene understanding
concepts.one_liner: Large language models like GPT-4V can interpret visual scenes by leveraging learned rules of perspective geometry and feature detection.
concepts.content:
GPT-4V can be used to interpret scenes by taking images as input and answering questions about them. At one level, it is a transformer trained on massive data using an autoregressive modeling objective. At another level, the transformer learns rules similar to classical vision: it detects edges in early layers, uses filters that act like wavelets tiling Fourier space, and reasons about perspective geometry to find vanishing points and estimate shape.

(see figure: 3D reconstruction using the simple visual system from @sec-simplesystem)
concepts.motivation_md: Explains how modern multimodal LLMs bridge the gap between raw pixel data and semantic/geometric understanding, showing that they often 're-discover' classical vision principles through massive data training.

concepts.title: Limitations of LLM-based scene reconstruction
concepts.one_liner: Current LLMs often fail to perfectly reconstruct images from text descriptions, revealing gaps in their fundamental understanding of scene consistency.
concepts.content:
Despite their accuracy in description, LLM-based scene reconstruction is not fully solved. When attempting to reconstruct an image from a text description, the output often looks incorrect, as seen in @fig-chatgpt_blockworld2. concepts.title: Unsolved solved computer vision problems
concepts.one_liner: Many computer vision problems that appear solved are actually illusions, with deeper challenges remaining hidden in the background.
concepts.content: Computer vision is making amazing progress, but one must beware of the "unsolved solved computer vision problems." For some vision tasks, it might appear as if a single method perfectly resolves the task or that foundational problems are solved. Often, this is just an illusion, and the problem was not really solved at all. Even when a problem is genuinely solved, there are many unsolved problems lurking in the background. Advances result from exploring new directions with an open mind and using creativity as a powerful tool.
concepts.motivation_md: Warns against complacency in research and engineering, reminding students that 'solved' benchmarks often hide edge cases and deeper complexities.

concepts.title: Hand-crafted vs. learning-based paradigms
concepts.one_liner: Hand-crafted models provide transparency and require no training data, while learning-based models offer superior generalization and robustness to environmental changes.
concepts.content:
Hand-crafted models provide a comprehensive understanding of system mechanisms, assumptions, and limitations. They require no training data and work immediately, but they are fragile and do not generalize outside their specific assumptions. When they fail, the cause is easy to identify, but that knowledge doesn't necessarily make the system work better.

Conversely, pretrained learning-based systems generalize to new settings and handle configurations outside their original modeling assumptions. They are robust to changes in illumination and do not rely on fragile, explicit operations like edge detection, though they may learn equivalent internal heuristics. Understanding these networks often requires experimental approaches similar to psychophysics in humans.

[FIGURE:2d5b0345de81fa09 | A split-screen conceptual illustration comparing two computer vision paradigms. The left side represents a hand-crafted model with rigid, mechanical gears, cogs, and circuit-like lines on a light...]

While GPT-4V can recognize geometric figures, its integration with rendering engines remains fragile. The field is evolving quickly, and the priority is to challenge existing approaches and identify relevant questions for new systems.

concepts.title: Recovering 3D World Coordinates from Depth
concepts.one_liner: 3D world coordinates for a pixel can be recovered from its image coordinates and depth using the inverse of the camera matrix.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique allows us to map 2D image pixels back into their original 3D spatial positions, which is essential for tasks like 3D reconstruction, navigation, and spatial reasoning in computer vision.
concepts.recap_md: - Use the inverse camera matrix $\mathbf{K}^{-1}$ to back-project 2D coordinates.

concepts.title: Camera Matrix Decomposition (K = MR)
concepts.one_liner: The camera matrix $\mathbf{K}$ accounts for focal length, image size, camera center, and rotation relative to world coordinates.
concepts.content:
The camera parameters will have to account for the focal length, image size, camera center, and the camera rotation with respect to the world coordinates:
$$\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{M} \mathbf{R}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Decomposing the camera matrix into intrinsic and extrinsic components allows for a modular understanding of how internal camera properties and external orientation separately affect the image formation process.
concepts.recap_md: - The camera matrix $\mathbf{K}$ is the product of intrinsic parameters $\mathbf{M}$ and rotation $\mathbf{R}$.

slots.motivation: Decomposing the camera matrix into intrinsic and extrinsic components allows for a modular understanding of how internal camera properties and external orientation separately affect the image formation process.

concepts.title: Intrinsic Camera Parameters for Perspective Projection
concepts.one_liner: Intrinsic camera parameters for perspective projection are represented by a matrix $\mathbf{M}$ containing focal and center point information.
concepts.motivation_md: Intrinsic parameters define the internal geometry of the camera, such as how light is focused onto the sensor and where the optical center lies, which is necessary for accurate 3D-to-2D mapping.
concepts.recap_md: - The matrix $\mathbf{M}$ encodes the focal length $a$ and the camera center $(n_0, m_0)$.

concepts.title: Extrinsic Camera Parameters for 3D Rotation
concepts.one_liner: Extrinsic camera parameters model the 3D rotation of the camera, often focusing on the rotation around the X-axis.
concepts.motivation_md: Extrinsic parameters describe the camera's position and orientation in the world, allowing the system to relate the camera's local view to a global coordinate frame.
concepts.recap_md: - The rotation matrix $\mathbf{R}$ defines the camera's orientation relative to the world.

concepts.title: Heuristic Parameter Selection for Depth Mapping
concepts.one_liner: Heuristic parameter selection provides a simpler alternative to formal calibration for defining camera constants.
concepts.content:
In order to apply the recovery of world coordinates, we need to define certain parameters: $d_0$, $n_0$, $m_0$, $a$, and $\theta$. Although we could determine these parameters using a calibration image, in this case, we'll opt for a simpler heuristic approach:

- $d_0$: We will set this value to 0.
- $n_0, m_0$: Defines the camera center point, where $n_0=N/2$ and $m_0=M/2$, when $N \times M$ is the input image size.
- $a$: Accounts for the image size and the camera focal length. One standard setting is to make $a = N$, where $N$ is the image width.
concepts.motivation_md: Formal camera calibration can be complex and requires specific calibration targets; heuristics provide a 'good enough' starting point for 3D reconstruction when exact parameters are unknown.
concepts.recap_md: - Set the camera center $(n_0, m_0)$ to the midpoint of the image dimensions.

slots.motivation: Formal camera calibration can be complex and requires specific calibration targets; heuristics provide a 'good enough' starting point for 3D reconstruction when exact parameters are unknown.
slots.key_passage: - Set the camera center $(n_0, m_0)$ to the midpoint of the image dimensions.

concepts.title: Ground plane angle theta
concepts.one_liner: The parameter $\theta$ represents the angle between the optical camera axis and the ground plane.
concepts.content: $\theta$ represents the angle between the optical camera axis and the ground plane. It would be possible to estimate this angle accurately by determining the direction of the surface normal in pixels corresponding to the ground and measuring the angle with respect to the vertical axis. However, for our purposes, we will simply set it to $\theta = \pi / 4$, as this is approximately the angle at which the pictures were taken.
concepts.motivation_md: Knowing the tilt of the camera relative to the ground is crucial for correctly orienting the reconstructed 3D scene so that 'down' in the model matches 'down' in the real world.

concepts.title: Learning-based 3D reconstruction
concepts.one_liner: Learning-based 3D reconstruction uses neural networks to directly transform images into world coordinates without manual feature detection.
concepts.content: Learning-based 3D reconstruction involves applying a neural network to an input image to obtain the output disparity and then transforming that disparity into world coordinates. Unlike traditional methods, we do not have to detect edges or any other manual features. Instead, the neural network learns to compute whatever features it deems necessary to solve the task. In this approach, we do not retrain the network using images from our simple visual world, but rely on its learned representations.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional 3D reconstruction relies on hand-crafted features like edges, which can be fragile; neural networks can learn more robust features automatically from large datasets.
concepts.recap_md: - Neural networks can output disparity maps directly from raw images.

concepts.title: Concluding Remarks on Giving Talks
concepts.one_liner: Preparation and rehearsal are the best cures for nervousness and ensure an enjoyable presentation for the audience.
concepts.content: Preparation and practice are essential for giving a successful talk. During the presentation, it is important to let the audience see your enjoyment of the work. Engaging with various resources and tips can help you find a personal style that works best. Ultimately, thorough preparation and rehearsal are the most effective ways to manage nervousness about public speaking.
concepts.motivation_md: Public speaking is a common source of anxiety. This concept provides a practical solution: rigorous preparation and the outward expression of enthusiasm to improve both the speaker's confidence and the audience's experience.

concepts.title: Introduction to the Revisited Simple Vision System
concepts.one_liner: Modern computer vision leverages large-scale pretrained models to solve complex visual tasks with minimal fine-tuning.
concepts.content: The emergence of large-scale pretrained models like DALL-E, GPT, and ChatGPT has shifted the approach to computer vision. These models are trained on massive, diverse datasets, allowing them to generalize across domains such as natural language processing, image generation, and depth perception. They can be used as standalone systems or as building blocks in more complex architectures. While these models produce astonishing results, a gap remains in building truly reliable and robust systems, raising the question of whether current optimism in the field is well-founded or premature.
concepts.motivation_md: The field of computer vision has moved from hand-crafted algorithms to leveraging massive pretrained models. Understanding this shift is crucial for using state-of-the-art tools effectively while remaining aware of their current limitations.
concepts.recap_md: - Large-scale pretrained models can solve diverse tasks with little to no fine-tuning.

concepts.title: MiDaS Model for 3D Perception
concepts.one_liner: MiDaS is a state-of-the-art neural network trained end-to-end to recover 3D scene structure from a single image.
concepts.content:
The MiDaS model represents the current state of the art for recovering three-dimensional (3D) structure from a single image. Unlike traditional algorithms derived from first principles of image formation, MiDaS is a neural network trained end-to-end using diverse real-world images with ground truth depth information and stereo images. From a user's perspective, it functions as a simple call, though utilizing it effectively requires understanding its training, output format, and how to adapt it to specific tasks.

(see figure: Image from the simple world.)
concepts.motivation_md: Recovering 3D information from a 2D image is an under-determined problem. MiDaS provides a powerful, pretrained solution that bypasses the need to manually derive complex geometric algorithms for every new scene.

concepts.title: Invariant Loss in Depth Prediction
concepts.one_liner: Invariant loss allows models to be trained on diverse datasets by ignoring ambiguities in scale and camera parameters.
concepts.content:
When training a model on a mix of diverse datasets, ambiguities arise regarding overall scale, camera parameters, and stereo baselines. To handle this, an invariant loss is used, which makes the training process more robust to these variations. While this improves the model's ability to learn from varied data sources, it also results in an output that is less convenient to use directly because the absolute scale is not preserved.

(see figure: Images and depth maps from the training set. *Source*: Image from @Ranftl2022)
concepts.motivation_md: Different depth datasets use different scales and cameras. Invariant loss allows a single model to learn from all of them simultaneously without being confused by these technical inconsistencies.
concepts.recap_md: - Invariant loss handles ambiguities in scale and camera parameters across datasets.

concepts.title: Disparity Prediction in Neural Networks
concepts.one_liner: The model predicts disparity, which is inverse depth up to an unknown scale and shift.
concepts.content: To manage the ambiguities inherent in diverse training data, the model is designed to predict disparity rather than absolute depth. Disparity is defined as inverse depth up to an unknown scale and shift. Because of this, the raw output of the model cannot be used directly as a physical measurement and must first be converted into world coordinates.
concepts.motivation_md: Predicting absolute depth is difficult when training data lacks a consistent scale. Predicting disparity allows the model to focus on relative depth relationships, which are more consistent across different images.
concepts.recap_md: - Disparity is the inverse of depth, subject to an unknown scale and shift.

slots.motivation: Predicting absolute depth is difficult when training data lacks a consistent scale. Predicting disparity allows the model to focus on relative depth relationships, which are more consistent across different images.
slots.key_passage: - Disparity is the inverse of depth, subject to an unknown scale and shift.

concepts.title: Converting Disparity to Depth Values
concepts.one_liner: To convert disparity to depth, the inverse of the disparity plus an unknown constant is calculated.
concepts.content:
MiDaS returns disparity values that are accurate only up to an unknown constant ($d_0$). To transform these values into world coordinates ($X, Y, Z$), we must apply camera intrinsic and extrinsic parameters. Specifically, to translate the returned disparity for a pixel $d[n,m]$ into a depth value $z[n,m]$, the disparity must be inverted after adding the constant:

$$\begin{aligned}z [n,m] = \frac{1}{ d [n,m] + d_0}\end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Raw model outputs are often in a relative format (disparity). This technique is necessary to recover actual physical distances (depth) required for 3D reconstruction or robotics applications.
concepts.recap_md: - Depth is calculated by inverting the sum of the predicted disparity and a constant $d_0$.

slots.motivation: Raw model outputs are often in a relative format (disparity). This technique is necessary to recover actual physical distances (depth) required for 3D reconstruction or robotics applications.
slots.key_passage: - Depth is calculated by inverting the sum of the predicted disparity and a constant $d_0$.
